title: US hiring slows as families face rising prices
summary:
US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, fewer than economists expected. The unemployment rate rose from 4.1 percent in August to 4.2 percent. This rate measures the share of people in the labor force who are without work and looking for a job.

The report matters to families because jobs provide income to pay for food, housing and other needs. But one month's figures do not tell the whole story.

Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, told PBS NewsHour that monthly job numbers can change a lot. She said employers added an average of 41,000 jobs each month over the past year. She said unemployment had stayed low and fairly steady, while recognizing that losing a job can be painful.

Hammack's bigger concern is inflation. Inflation means prices are rising overall. If pay grows more slowly than prices, a family's money buys less.

She said people she met in Northeast Ohio described difficult choices about paying for food, fuel and rent. Some were relying more on credit, or borrowed money.

The Federal Reserve works toward both strong employment and stable prices. Its inflation goal is 2 percent. Hammack said bringing inflation back to that goal remains important. The hiring report arrives a month before the US midterm elections.
why_it_matters: Jobs help families pay for everyday needs. Rising prices can make those needs harder to afford when pay does not keep up.
